candidateRows: Human moral, existential, social, and cosmological problems would remain unchanged if every supernatural religion were disproved.
This directly contests the proposition that Christian theism is necessary to explain morality, purpose, social obligation, or humanity's central questions.
After recounting a novel in which disproving the resurrection causes social collapse, Hitchens argues that disbelief would leave humanity facing precisely the same moral and existential tasks.
Even granting a deistic first cause leaves the theist unable to establish knowledge of a deity's will, commands, or intentions.
The argument separates a possible creator from revealed religion and places the decisive evidentiary burden on claims to know divine purposes and commands.
Hitchens distinguishes deism from theism, provisionally concedes that a creator could explain origins, and argues that no human can thereby claim access to divine wishes or moral rules.
Naturalistic explanations are evidence-responsive and falsifiable, whereas theistic belief lacks evidence and indefinitely replenishes itself through faith.
This supplies Hitchens's core epistemic case for preferring naturalism over theism by contrasting evidence and possible falsification with insulated faith.
Hitchens rejects even a divine first cause, contrasts submission to physical and biological evidence with belief in design, and argues that theism specifies no possible disconfirming evidence.
The immense extinction, suffering, and delayed religious intervention portrayed by theism make God appear cruel, incompetent, and unworthy of worship.
The argument directly denies divine greatness through natural evil, evolutionary waste, human misery, and the alleged inadequacy of revealed redemptive interventions.
Hitchens invokes species extinction and most of human prehistory's suffering, then contrasts that history with late and implausible religious interventions to indict the proposed designer.
Evils committed in God's name do not disprove God's greatness, just as abuses of science do not disprove science's value.
This answers the debate's religion-poisons-everything thesis by separating a belief system's truth or value from wrongdoing committed by professed adherents.
Hitchens's contention that religious wrongdoing shows God is not great and that religion poisons human life.

Lennox accepts condemnation of religious evils but distinguishes those acts from God's character, compares them with technological abuses of Einstein's science, and notes atrocities by atheist regimes.
Science describes mechanisms but does not eliminate the need for a creator who explains why an ordered, intelligible universe exists.
This advances the principal theistic explanation of existence and order while directly rejecting the alleged incompatibility between scientific and divine explanations.
Hitchens's position that scientific investigation has displaced religion as an explanation and makes a divine creator unnecessary.
Lennox distinguishes mechanism from agency, argues that scientific laws do not create what they describe, invokes cosmic existence and order, and links early science to belief in a lawgiver.
Atheistic naturalism cannot justify trust in human reason, while theism grounds both the universe's intelligibility and minds capable of knowing it.
This challenges the coherence of Hitchens's evidential worldview and presents a creator as the rational foundation for scientific inquiry and reliable cognition.
Hitchens's contrast between evidence-responsive naturalism and faith-based theism, including his claim that faith diminishes truth or value.

Lennox argues that science presupposes faith in intelligibility, calls Hitchens's dismissal of faith self-undermining, and claims unguided evolution supplies no basis for trusting truth-directed cognition.
Scientism cannot answer questions of meaning or value, and atheism erodes human dignity, freedom, and ultimate hope.
The move directly supports the motion's dignity-and-hope dimensions by contrasting humans made in God's image with products of blind, purposeless processes.
Lennox acknowledges science's importance but stresses its limits concerning meaning and value, then argues that abolishing God leaves humans without nobility, freedom, or enduring hope.
Christianity historically and conceptually grounds liberty, conscience, human rights, democracy, universities, and protections for dissent.
This provides a distinct historical and philosophical argument that Christian theism sustains important institutions and values associated with human dignity and freedom.
Lennox appeals to an atheist social theorist's account of Christianity's foundational role and adds that Christian institutions educated and legally protected modern atheist critics.
Atheistic naturalism cannot sustain the objective moral standard required to condemn God as tyrannical or morally bad.
This directly challenges the anti-theistic moral indictment by arguing that blind evolutionary processes cannot yield objective obligation, responsibility, justice, good, or evil.
Hitchens's moral indictment of God as a cruel, capricious, incompetent designer and an unacceptable eternal authority.
Lennox rejects the deity Hitchens depicts, notes that atheism does not prevent tyranny, and argues that moral condemnation becomes groundless if values and agency are products of blind forces.
Lennox claims knowledge beyond what he can establish and misuses Einstein by blurring impersonal cosmic order with belief in a personal, revelatory God.
The move directly attacks the epistemic warrant and scientific-authority component of the Christian-theist case.
Lennox's appeal to scientific intelligibility, Einstein, and confident knowledge of a personal saving God.
Hitchens begins his rebuttal by challenging Lennox's certainty and distinguishing Einstein's impersonal conception of cosmic order from Christian theism.
Cosmic expansion, eventual destruction, and humanity's minute place in the universe undermine claims that the cosmos was purposefully designed for human redemption.
This move contests the design and purpose claims at the center of Lennox's scientific case for divine greatness.
Lennox's claim that cosmic existence and intelligibility are best explained by a purposeful divine creator.
Hitchens invokes expansion, stellar and planetary extinction, cosmic emptiness, and humanity's vulnerability to dispute a human-centered providential design.
An eternal omniscient father would constitute an inescapable dictatorship that surveils thought, creates humans morally defective, and threatens punishment for that defect.
The argument directly supports the anti-theistic claim that the proposed God is tyrannical rather than great or liberating.
Lennox's portrayal of God as a loving father, righteous judge, and source of meaningful human freedom.
Hitchens argues that divine omniscience and judgment amount to permanent domination and also authorize human rulers who claim divine sanction.
Religious faith supplies no uniquely moral action available only to believers, while it can uniquely motivate grave harms performed specifically because of faith.
The paired challenge directly contests the claim that objective morality requires God and reverses it into an indictment of faith.
Lennox's argument that atheism cannot rationally ground moral values and that morality ultimately depends upon God.
Hitchens asks for a good act unavailable to nonbelievers and contrasts that absence with harms he attributes specifically to religious commitment.
Confidence about God need not be arrogant certainty if God has revealed himself, and Christianity stands or falls on evidence that Jesus is God incarnate and rose from death.
This move supplies the principal epistemic bridge from general theism to the specifically Christian claim about God's greatness.
Hitchens's charge that Lennox claims inaccessible knowledge and that religious certainty is epistemically unwarranted.
Lennox distinguishes arrogance from accepting disclosed evidence, then identifies incarnation and resurrection as the decisive evidence for Christian revelation.
Atheists can recognize and perform good because all humans bear God's image, while Christ's unique self-sacrifice supplies the distinctively Christian moral act.
The move answers a signature anti-theistic challenge while preserving the theistic grounding of universal human moral capacity.
Hitchens's demand for a morally good action a believer can perform that an atheist cannot perform.
Lennox first explains shared moral ability through the divine image, then redirects the uniqueness question to Christ's atoning death.
Religious violence and coercion are not accidental abuses but direct consequences of supernatural belief, especially belief in a divine dictatorship.
This proposition states the core causal indictment underlying the anti-theistic case against religion and divine authority.
Lennox's suggestion that violent or oppressive conduct is merely behavior undertaken in religion's name.
Hitchens corrects the characterization of his position and argues that harmful authoritarian conduct follows from supernatural and dictatorial premises themselves.
Violence committed in Christ's name is a perversion rather than an expression of Christianity because Christ prohibited physical force and defined his kingdom as nonworldly.
The move directly contests the causal link between Christian doctrine and religious violence asserted by Hitchens.
Hitchens's claim that coercive and violent behavior is innate in religion rather than an abuse of it.
Lennox concedes misconduct by professing Christians but argues that such conduct disobeys Christ and therefore misrepresents Christianity's defining source.
Jesus's teachings contain coercive, authoritarian, and potentially wicked demands, so Christianity cannot excuse religious oppression by appealing to Christ's character or commands.
The move attacks Lennox's proposed distinction between authentic Christianity and coercive distortions at its claimed doctrinal source.
Lennox's assertion that Christ forbade coercion and that violent Christians merely disobey authentic Christianity.
Hitchens cites severe sayings attributed to Jesus and argues that their acceptability depends entirely on accepting otherwise questionable messianic claims.
The Gospel case for Jesus is weakened by reverse-engineered prophecy fulfillment and by the rejection of his messianic claim by the nearer Jewish authorities.
The move directly challenges the evidential foundation Lennox offers for preferring Christianity over rival religious explanations.
Lennox's claim that evidence concerning Jesus's life, death, and resurrection establishes Christianity over rival faiths.
Hitchens argues that Gospel narratives were shaped to satisfy known prophecies and that competing Jewish and Christian messianic claims lack credible warrant.
Jesus claimed divinity, fulfilled historically embedded prophecy, and uniquely embodied the promised sacrifice for human sin.
The move directly defends the historical and theological credibility of Christianity against the charge that its prophecies and miracle claims are fabricated superstition.
Hitchens's claim that Gospel prophecy is reverse-engineered and that Jesus neither claimed divinity nor warranted messianic belief.
After Hitchens characterizes Christian prophecy as reverse-engineered Bronze Age superstition, Lennox disputes both the account of Jesus's claims and the dismissal of prophecy.
Miracle claims are less credible than ordinary natural explanations, and respected Christian apologetics do not establish that Jesus claimed divinity.
The move supplies the epistemic standard behind the anti-theistic rejection of virgin birth and divinity claims rather than merely expressing disbelief.
Lennox's defense of the virgin conception as a unique divine miracle and his assertion that Jesus explicitly claimed to be God.
Hitchens answers Lennox's miracle defense by contrasting supernatural suspension with ordinary deception and invoking a Christian apologist against the divinity claim.
Human concern, solidarity, duty, affection, and love can arise from social and evolutionary life without requiring belief in God.
The move directly presents an anti-theistic explanation of human dignity and moral solidarity, one of the principal explanatory questions named by the motion.
Asked whether humanity has dignity, meaning, hope, or value, Hitchens rejects the proposed dilemma and grounds care in species survival and human social bonds.
Only creation in God's image rationally secures unique and infinite human value against evolutionary views that reduce humans to other animals.
This is the principal Christian-theist account of human dignity and explicitly argues that abandoning divine-image status imperils the moral valuation of persons.
Hitchens's claim that evolved human solidarity and reciprocal social bonds can explain care and responsibility without a divine source.
Lennox agrees that moral feelings are present but argues that the decisive issue is their rational foundation, contrasting divine image-bearing with Singer's conclusions.
Genetic and behavioral continuity with other animals makes the claim that humans uniquely bear God's image explanatorily empty.
The move attacks the factual premise of Lennox's dignity argument by challenging the alleged categorical boundary between humans and other animals.
Lennox's assertion that humans possess infinite and categorically unique value because they alone are created in the image of God.
Hitchens acknowledges excesses in animal-rights advocacy but uses animal social capacities and genomic kinship to reject a uniquely divine human status.
Observed natural selection should be distinguished from unguided origins, because the language-like information in DNA supports an inference to intelligence.
The argument provides Lennox's central scientific case that biological information is better explained by intelligence than by wholly mindless evolutionary processes.
Asked about mistrust of evolution, Lennox accepts observable variation through natural selection but disputes the sufficiency of unguided processes for life's origin and information.
People leaving theism can find greater inspiration in literature, philosophy, science, and secular transcendence while retaining morality and responsibility.
The move offers a constructive anti-theistic account of meaning, beauty, consolation, morality, and responsibility after supernatural belief is abandoned.

Responding to a question about leaving theism while remaining in a religious institution, Hitchens recommends secular sources of wonder and frames post-religious transcendence as a civilizational task.
Christ's divine identity makes his self-sacrificial atonement coherent, life-giving, and the basis for the claim that God is immeasurably great.
The move directly answers the motion through Christianity's central claim about Christ's divinity, sacrificial death, forgiveness, protective love, and divine greatness.
Hitchens's rejection of vicarious redemption as immoral scapegoating and his mocking interpretation of the biblical shepherd-and-sheep image.
Near the end of his closing statement, Lennox argues that atonement would be outrageous if Jesus were merely human but is unique because Jesus is divine.
The proposed example of uniquely Christian morality fails because divine self-sacrifice presupposes exceptional status and leaves the morality of vicarious redemption unresolved.
The move renews a core moral objection to Christianity by arguing that the offered counterexample neither answers the believer-versus-unbeliever test nor validates atonement.
Lennox's proposed answer that a believer could perform the uniquely moral act of offering himself as a sacrifice for humanity's redemption.
Hitchens opens his closing by refusing consolation and revisiting his unanswered moral challenge, arguing that Lennox's sacrificial example contains a decisive qualification.
Attributing every mystery or transcendent experience to God is a tautological non-explanation that removes the need for inquiry without adding knowledge.
The move attacks the explanatory value of theism itself, contending that divine attribution neither explains transcendence nor improves on acknowledged uncertainty.
Lennox's repeated inference that transcendent experience, aesthetics, moral awareness, and other unexplained features point upward to a divine mind.
Using the preceding naval story as setup, Hitchens warns that assigning all mystery to supernatural purpose makes everything trivially explicable and adds no understanding.
European fascism cannot fairly be classified as secular or atheist because its regimes and movements were entwined with Catholic institutions and non-atheistic pagan beliefs.
This directly contests the use of twentieth-century dictatorships as evidence that atheism produces political oppression and mass wrongdoing.
The earlier contention that atheist regimes of the twentieth century demonstrate the destructive moral consequences of atheism.

After finishing a preceding argument about transcendence, Hitchens explicitly turns to the challenge concerning atheist regimes and discusses fascism's institutional and ideological religious connections.
Stalinism reproduced religious structures of authority, credulity, heresy enforcement, and personal veneration, so Soviet tyranny should not be treated as straightforward secular atheism.
The argument supplies a distinct Soviet counterexample to the claim that atheist ideology itself accounts for totalitarian violence and political worship.
The earlier appeal to Soviet and other avowedly atheist regimes as proof that atheism generates totalitarian cruelty.
Following his discussion of fascism, Hitchens shifts to Russia and argues that Stalin exploited inherited religious habits and recreated quasi-religious institutions and iconography.
Christian participation in abolition does not establish Christianity as the source of morality because Christianity had long justified slavery and moral opposition also arose outside the faith.
This directly challenges the Christian-theist account of moral grounding by arguing that human morality can precede and correct religious teaching.
The earlier invocation of William Wilberforce and Christian abolitionism as evidence that Christian faith grounds moral progress.

Hitchens concedes Wilberforce's Christian motivation but contrasts it with Christianity's historical defense of slavery, non-Christian abolitionists, and religion's delayed accommodation to moral change.
